chunks: "The difference is how the receiver knows when to sample. In a synchronous link like SPI or I2C there's a clock signal shared between the two sides.
The transmitter changes data on one edge and the receiver samples on the other, so the sampling instant is directly tied to the data.
It doesn't matter exactly how fast the clock runs; it can even stop and start.
The costs are an extra wire, and timing constraints like setup and hold, because the clock and data travel on different traces and can skew against each other.
In an asynchronous link like UART there's no clock wire. Both sides agree on a bit rate in advance and each uses its own oscillator.
The line idles high, a start bit marks the beginning of a byte, and the receiver then samples each bit at the centre of its time slot using its own clock, and a stop bit finishes the frame.

The trade-off: you save a wire and it tolerates long cables, but you pay about 20% overhead for the start and stop bits, and the two clocks must agree within a few percent or the sample point walks out of the bit by the end of the byte.
So sync gives you speed and low overhead; async gives you simplicity and fewer wires."
